sections.title: Single node: leases, watches and durability

stages.name: Lamport clocks
hints: Topic `lamport`: keep one counter per process and hand it out with `send`
A local event and a send both increment the counter before it is used
On receive the counter becomes max(local, received) + 1 — the +1 is the whole point
Counters never go backwards, even when a message arrives from the past

tests.name: a fresh process has not ticked yet
a local event moves the clock on by one
a send stamps the counter it has just moved
a receive takes the maximum plus one
a receive never moves the clock backwards
reading the clock does not move it
each process keeps a counter of its own
an exchange orders cause before effect
a message from far in the future drags the clock with it
a long seeded exchange matches the tester's own replay

examples.title: Two processes exchanging one message
examples.request:
a send on `a`, a message stamped 7 delivered to `b`, and both clocks read back

./your_program.sh lamport
send a
recv b 7
get b
get a
examples.note: The trap is the +1. `b` had never ticked, so the merge alone would leave it at 7 — the same instant as the send it is supposed to follow. The extra tick is what makes the receive strictly later than the send, and `get` must not add another.

examples.title: A message that arrives from the past
examples.request:
a clock pushed to 3, then a message stamped 1 delivered to it

./your_program.sh lamport
local a
local a
local a
recv a 1
get a
examples.note: A Lamport clock is monotonic per process, so an old message can never pull one back. Writing `ts + 1` instead of `max(local, ts) + 1` passes every test where messages happen to arrive in order and fails the moment one is late.

stages.name: Vector clocks and causal comparison
hints: Topic `vector-clock`: a map from process name to counter, and a missing entry is a zero
`cmp` answers before, after, equal or concurrent — four cases, not three
Merging on receive takes the componentwise maximum, then increments the receiver's own entry
Two clocks are concurrent when neither dominates: test both directions

tests.name: a process that has done nothing has an empty clock
a local event moves only the entry of the process that acted
a receive merges componentwise and then increments the receiver
a name nobody mentions counts as zero
cmp names all four relations
a clock is equal to itself
before and after are mirrors, and concurrent is symmetric
a delivered message is strictly behind the clock that received it
a merge never lowers a component
every pair of a seeded exchange agrees with the oracle

examples.title: A message from `a` delivered to `b`
examples.request:
`a` ticks twice and sends; the message is delivered to `b`; both are read back

./your_program.sh vector-clock
local a
send a
recv b {"a":2}
get b
get a
examples.note: The receiver's own entry is incremented *after* the merge, and only its own. A receive that increments every entry, or that increments before merging, still looks plausible on one exchange and orders nothing correctly on two.

examples.title: Four comparisons, one per relation
examples.note: The third comparison is the one that catches a map compared by equality: {"a":1} and {"a":1,"b":0} are the same clock written two ways. Compare the union of the names, not the keys of either side.

stages.name: Version vectors and sibling detection
hints: Topic `version-vector`: a value carries the vector of the replica that wrote it
A write that does not dominate an existing value creates a sibling instead of replacing it
Sync merges both replicas' sets and drops any value dominated by another
Siblings come back sorted so two replicas that agree answer identically

tests.name: a first write stamps the writing replica, and nothing else
a second write on the same replica replaces the first
two replicas writing apart fork into siblings
a sync leaves both replicas holding the same set
siblings come back sorted and deduplicated
a write that has seen every sibling replaces them all
put-ctx naming the whole context collapses the siblings
put-ctx naming a stale context forks again
a fresh process shares nothing with the one before it
a three-way fork keeps all three values

examples.title: Two replicas writing at the same time
examples.request:
one write on each replica, no communication between them, then a sync

./your_program.sh version-vector
put r1 cart red
put r2 cart blue
sync r1 r2
read r1 cart
read r2 cart
examples.note: Neither vector dominates the other — {"r1":1} and {"r2":1} are concurrent — so the sync has no basis for dropping either. Picking the later arrival, or the larger replica name, silently loses a write; that is the bug this whole stage exists to catch.

examples.title: Resolving the siblings with put-ctx
examples.request:
a write that names, as its context, the merge of both siblings' vectors

./your_program.sh version-vector
put r1 cart red
put r2 cart blue
sync r1 r2
put-ctx r1 cart purple {"r1":1,"r2":1}
read r1 cart
examples.note: The context is the claim "I read both of these". Increment the writer's own entry on top of it and the result dominates both siblings, so both are dropped. A write that ignores the context it was given cannot collapse anything, and the siblings accumulate for ever.

stages.name: Hybrid logical clocks
hints: Topic `hlc`: a timestamp is (l, c) — a physical part and a counter that breaks ties
`now` takes l = max(l, wall); when l did not move, c increments, otherwise c resets to 0
`recv` takes l = max(l, l_local, l_msg) and picks c from whichever source it matched
The result must be strictly greater than both the local clock and the message's

tests.name: a fresh clock takes the wall clock it is handed
the counter counts a stall and resets when the physical part moves
a wall clock that goes backwards never drags the clock back
reading the clock does not move it
a receive adopts a message from the future
a receive of a stale message keeps the local physical part
equal physical parts take the larger counter plus one
each process carries its own pair
a receive dominates both the local clock and the message
a seeded sequence is strictly increasing in (l, c)

examples.title: A wall clock that stalls, then jumps, then slips
examples.request:
five readings of a clock whose physical part stands still and then goes back

./your_program.sh hlc
now a 100
now a 100
now a 100
now a 200
now a 150
examples.note: The counter is not a count of events; it is what orders events the physical part cannot separate. It resets the moment `l` moves, which is what keeps it small and bounded rather than growing for the lifetime of the process.

examples.title: A message from a node whose clock is ahead
examples.request:
a message stamped (500, 3) delivered to a process whose wall clock reads 10

./your_program.sh hlc
recv b 10 500 3
get b
now b 100
examples.note: The receive has to beat the message, not merely match it, so the counter that came with the message is incremented. Taking `max(c_local, c_msg)` without the +1 gives a timestamp equal to one already used elsewhere, and two different events then share an instant.

stages.name: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes
hints: Topic `consistent-hash`: place `vnodes` points per node on a ring and walk clockwise
`locate` is a function: the same key must always answer the same node
Virtual nodes are what makes the load even — one point per node is visibly lumpy
`stats` reports how many of the sampled keys landed on each node

tests.name: a key always lands on the same node
a key only ever lands on a node that is on the ring
one node owns every key
the answer does not drift while the ring stands still
virtual nodes spread the keys evenly
one point per node is visibly lumpier
stats counts every sampled key exactly once
an empty ring answers instead of crashing
removing a node that was never added leaves the ring alone

examples.title: A two-node ring and one key
examples.request:
two nodes with the default 128 points each, then the same key located twice

./your_program.sh consistent-hash
add n1 128
add n2 128
locate user-42
locate user-42
examples.note: Which node answers is your hash's business and no test here predicts it. That the second answer equals the first is not: `locate` is a pure function of the key and the current membership.

examples.title: What the virtual nodes are for
examples.request:
four nodes, then where `key0`..`key3999` land

./your_program.sh consistent-hash
add n1 128
add n2 128
add n3 128
add n4 128
stats 4000
examples.note: Run the same thing with `add n1 1` and the counts stop looking like quarters: four random points on a ring cut it into four very unequal arcs, and the arc is the share of the key space. That is the whole reason for the points.

stages.name: Key movement when the ring changes
hints: Adding a node may only take keys, never shuffle keys between two nodes that stayed
Removing a node may only give its keys away; everything else stays put
Roughly 1/N of the keys move when the Nth node joins — that is the whole point
Re-adding a node that was removed must restore the mapping exactly

tests.name: adding a node never shuffles keys between the nodes that stayed
every key that moves when a node joins moves to that node
removing a node only moves the keys it owned
roughly one key in N moves when the Nth node joins
removing a node and adding it back restores the mapping exactly
three joins in a row still never shuffle a key between survivors
a node leaving and a node joining only touch their own keys
the order the nodes joined in does not change where a key lands

examples.title: A fourth node joins
examples.request:
three nodes, a key located, a fourth node, the same key located again

./your_program.sh consistent-hash
add n1 128
add n2 128
add n3 128
locate user-42
add n4 128
locate user-42
examples.note: A key may only stay where it is or move to `n4`. If `user-42` had been on `n1` and answered `n2` after the join, the ring is not consistent hashing — it is `hash(key) % n` wearing a costume, and every key in the store would be in the wrong place after a join.

examples.title: A node leaves and comes back
examples.request:
a key located before a removal, during it, and after the node is back

./your_program.sh consistent-hash
add n1 128
add n2 128
add n3 128
locate user-42
remove n2
locate user-42
add n2 128
locate user-42
examples.note: The points a node owns have to be derived from its name, not from when it joined or from a counter. Seed a random generator per `add` and this last `locate` answers something else, which means every key that node held is lost after a restart.

stages.name: Rendezvous (HRW) hashing
hints: Topic `rendezvous`: score every node for the key and take the highest
No ring and no virtual nodes: the score function does all the work
`locate-k` returns the top k in score order, and its head is what `locate` answers
Removing a node only moves the keys it owned, exactly as a ring does

tests.name: the head of locate-k is what locate answers
locate-k ranks every node once, with no repeats
asking for more nodes than there are returns every one
the same key ranks the nodes the same way every time
one node owns every key
adding a node only takes keys, it never shuffles them
removing a node only moves the keys it owned
removing the best node promotes the runner-up
removing a node leaves the others in the same order
locating with no nodes answers instead of crashing

examples.title: Scoring one key against three nodes
examples.request:
three nodes, the whole ranking for one key, then the plain lookup

./your_program.sh rendezvous
add n1
add n2
add n3
locate-k user-42 3
locate user-42
examples.note: `locate` is not a second implementation. It is `locate-k <key> 1` with the brackets taken off, and the suite checks exactly that: a head that disagrees with the ranking means two different score functions are in the program.

examples.title: A node leaves
examples.request:
the ranking for a key, then the same ranking without `n1`

./your_program.sh rendezvous
add n1
add n2
add n3
locate-k user-42 3
remove n1
locate-k user-42 3
locate user-42
examples.note: This is what rendezvous buys over a ring: not only do the survivors keep their keys, the *replicas* keep their order, so a key whose owner died already knows which node takes over without asking anybody.

stages.name: Quorum math: N, R, W and overlap
hints: Topic `quorum`: a read and a write quorum overlap when R + W > N
Two writes can conflict when 2W <= N — that is a different question from overlap
The smallest read quorum that always sees the latest write is N - W + 1
Answer for the numbers you were given, not for the defaults

tests.name: a read and a write overlap exactly when R + W is more than N
two writes can conflict exactly when 2W is at most N
the smallest read quorum is N - W + 1
the three-replica settings everyone quotes
the edges: reading from nobody, writing to everybody, a single replica
a seeded sweep of larger triples agrees with the arithmetic
a larger read quorum never loses an overlap it already had
the same triple always gets the same answer

examples.title: The three-replica settings
examples.request:
N = 3 with the three settings a store actually ships with

./your_program.sh quorum
check 3 2 2
check 3 1 2
check 3 3 1
examples.note: `overlap` and `write_conflict` answer different questions and a program that derives one from the other is wrong on the third line: R = 3, W = 1 reads from everybody, so every read sees every write, while two writes of one replica each can land on different nodes and neither will ever see the other.

examples.title: Writing to everybody, reading from one
examples.request:
the two extremes of N = 5, and the degenerate single replica

./your_program.sh quorum
check 5 1 5
check 5 5 1
check 1 1 1
examples.note: `min_r` is N - W + 1 and nothing else: it is the smallest read that cannot miss a write of W, not the R that was passed in and not a majority. With W = N one replica is enough, which is exactly the trade a write-all store is making.

stages.name: Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff
hints: A sloppy quorum accepts a write on a node outside the preference list when a member is down
The stand-in records a hint naming the node the write really belongs to
When the real owner comes back, the hint is handed off and then forgotten
A sloppy quorum is not a quorum: it can lose the overlap guarantee, and must say so

tests.name: a write with every replica alive needs no stand-in
a write with a member down is accepted on a stand-in
the number of hints is exactly the number of replicas that were down
strict is false exactly when a stand-in was used
hints lists the keys a stand-in is holding
a handoff delivers every hint and leaves none
handing off twice delivers nothing the second time
a hint for an owner that never comes back is still held
an owner nobody hinted for is holding nothing

examples.title: A write while one replica is down
examples.request:
W = 3 of N = 3 with everybody up, then with one down, then W = 2 with one up

./your_program.sh quorum
sloppy 3 3 3
sloppy 3 3 2
sloppy 3 2 1
examples.note: All three writes are accepted, which is the whole point of being sloppy, but only the first one is a quorum write. The second and third were completed by a node outside the preference list, so the overlap argument from stage 08 does not cover them and `strict` has to say so.

examples.title: Hinted handoff
examples.request:
`n4` takes two writes belonging to `n1`, then `n1` comes back

./your_program.sh quorum
hint n1 n4 user-42
hint n1 n4 user-99
hints n1
handoff n1
hints n1
examples.note: A hint is per owner, and the handoff is what makes it temporary. A store that delivers the data but keeps the hint hands the same keys over again on the next handoff, and one that drops the hint without delivering has quietly lost a write that was acknowledged.

stages.name: Bloom filter
hints: Topic `bloom`: k hash positions per item over m bits, all set on add
`contains` is only ever 'maybe' or 'no': a false negative is a bug, never a tuning issue
The measured false-positive rate must sit inside the theoretical bound for m, k and n
Derive the k positions from one or two hashes; k independent hash functions are not needed

tests.name: init reports back the size it was given
an item that was added is always maybe
items that were never added are mostly not present
a false positive rate inside the theoretical bound
set bits grow with insertions and never exceed the filter
a filter with too few bits is useless but never loses an item
init a second time resets the filter
adding the same item twice changes nothing
the optimal number of hashes beats a badly chosen one

examples.title: A filter that is certain about what it holds
examples.request:
a 1024-bit filter with three positions per item, two items added, two asked about

./your_program.sh bloom
init 1024 3
add alpha
add beta
contains alpha
contains gamma
stats
examples.note: `contains` has two answers and neither of them is `yes`. `maybe` means every one of the k bits is set, which an item that was never added can also manage once the filter is full enough. `no` is the only certain answer a Bloom filter gives.

examples.title: What the filter will admit to
examples.request:
three items in a filter far too small for them, then its own accounting

./your_program.sh bloom
init 64 4
add one
add two
add three
stats
examples.note: set_bits is the honest measure of how full a filter is: it rises by at most k per add and by less once positions start colliding. When it approaches bits, every `contains` answers `maybe` and the filter has stopped saying anything.

stages.name: HyperLogLog
hints: Topic `hll`: 2^p registers, each holding the longest run of leading zeros it has seen
The estimate is the harmonic mean of the registers, times alpha times m squared
Small cardinalities need linear counting, or the estimate is badly wrong
The relative error must sit inside 1.04 / sqrt(2^p) over many trials

tests.name: count on an empty sketch is zero
init reports two to the power p registers
the estimate of a small set is close to exact
adding the same item a thousand times does not change the estimate
counting twice gives the same answer
the insertion order does not change the estimate
a mean relative error inside the standard-error envelope
a larger precision is not worse than a smaller one
init a second time resets the sketch

examples.title: A sketch counting four things, one of them twice
examples.request:
a sketch of 2^12 registers, five adds over four distinct items

./your_program.sh hll
init 12
add a
add b
add c
add b
add d
count
examples.note: Five adds, four distinct items, and the answer is the distinct count: a register only ever moves up to a longer run of zeros, so the second `add b` writes the same value it wrote the first time and changes nothing.

examples.title: Where the raw estimator cannot be trusted
examples.request:
one item in a sketch of 16 registers, then the same item in a sketch of 16384

./your_program.sh hll
init 4
add a
count
init 14
add a
count
examples.note: With one item in 16 registers the harmonic-mean estimator is wildly biased — it is asymptotic, and one item is not the asymptote. Linear counting over the registers still at zero is what makes a small set come back as itself, and the usual threshold to switch at is 2.5 m.

stages.name: Merkle tree build
hints: Topic `merkle`: leaf = sha256(0x00 || leaf bytes), node = sha256(0x01 || left hex || right hex)
An odd node at a level is carried up unchanged, not duplicated
The root changes when any leaf changes, and only then
The same leaves always produce the same root, whatever order they were added in

tests.name: the root of four leaves is the one the oracle computes
a tree of one leaf is that leaf's hash
the root of an empty tree is the hash of nothing
an odd number of leaves carries the last node up
level zero holds the leaf hashes
the top level holds the root
changing one leaf changes the root and nothing else
the same leaves always give the same root
trees of every size up to seventeen match the oracle
every node of every level matches the oracle

examples.title: A tree of four leaves, and the nodes under its root
examples.request:
four leaves, then the root and one node from each level

./your_program.sh merkle
build t a,b,c,d
root t
node t 0 0
node t 1 0
node t 2 0
examples.note: Level 0 is the leaves and the top level holds the single root, so `node t 2 0` and `root t` are the same string. `node t 0 0` is sha256(0x00 || "a") and nothing else: the 0x00 is what stops a leaf from ever colliding with a node.

examples.title: Three leaves, and the one that is carried up
examples.request:
an odd tree, then the lone node at level 1 and the leaf it came from

./your_program.sh merkle
build o a,b,c
node o 1 1
node o 0 2
root o
examples.note: `c` has no sibling, so it rises to level 1 untouched. Hashing it with itself instead would be the other obvious rule and gives a different root — and it is the rule behind the CVE-2012-2459 duplicate-transaction bug in Bitcoin, where two different leaf lists hash to the same tree.

stages.name: Merkle diff with the fewest round trips
hints: Compare roots first: equal roots mean equal trees and no further work
Descend only into subtrees whose hashes differ — that is the whole saving
Report the differing leaves as ranges, so a caller can fetch them in one go
Count the nodes you compared: a walk that visits everything has learnt nothing

tests.name: two identical trees diff to no ranges at all
diffing a tree against itself costs one comparison
one differing leaf is found exactly
adjacent differing leaves merge into one range
scattered differences match the ranges the oracle computes
a diff never looks at every node in the tree
a large tree with two scattered differences is still cheap
the diff is the same in both directions
two trees that differ everywhere report one whole range

examples.title: Two replicas that agree
examples.request:
two eight-leaf trees built from the same data

./your_program.sh merkle
build a a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h
build b a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h
diff a b
examples.note: The roots match, so there is nothing below them to look at. This is the case anti-entropy spends almost all of its time in, and it has to cost one hash comparison and not fifteen.

examples.title: Two replicas that disagree about one key
examples.request:
the same trees with leaf 5 changed on one side

./your_program.sh merkle
build a a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h
build b a,b,c,d,e,X,g,h
diff a b
examples.note: Seven is 1 + 2 per level: the root, then the two children at each of the three levels below it, of which only one differs and is followed. `compared` is the assertion this stage is really about — a diff that answers [[5,5]] after reading all fifteen nodes has done a linear scan with extra steps.

stages.name: G-Counter and PN-Counter
hints: Topics `g-counter` and `pn-counter`: one entry per replica, merged by maximum
A PN-Counter is two G-Counters: increments and decrements, never one signed number
Merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent — every delivery order converges
A replica only ever writes its own entry; it copies others by taking the maximum

tests.name: a fresh counter reads zero and then counts up
the value is the sum over every replica
a stale merge never lowers the value
merging the same state twice changes nothing
a replica writes only its own entry, so no increment is lost
every delivery order of the same updates converges
a pn-counter keeps increments and decrements apart
a pn-counter can go below zero
every delivery order of increments and decrements converges

examples.title: Two replicas counting in one process
examples.request:
two replicas increment their own entries, then the counter is read

./your_program.sh g-counter
inc r1 5
inc r2 7
value r1
state r1
examples.note: The shape of `state` is entirely yours: the harness never looks inside it, it only hands it to another replica's `merge`. What it must do is round trip, so whatever a replica needs to keep has to be in there.

examples.title: Increments and decrements are counted apart
examples.request:
one replica adds ten and takes three, then another takes twenty

./your_program.sh pn-counter
inc r1 10
dec r1 3
value r1
dec r2 20
value r1
examples.note: Storing 7 as a single number would be the bug. Two G-Counters merge by maximum on each half independently, and the difference is read at the end; one signed number has no maximum that means 'whoever saw more updates'.

stages.name: LWW-Register and OR-Set
hints: Topic `lww-register`: value plus timestamp, and a deterministic tie-break on equal timestamps
Topic `or-set`: an add carries a unique tag; a remove takes away the tags it saw
An add concurrent with a remove survives — that is the whole difference from a 2P-Set
Re-adding after a remove must work, which is why tags cannot be reused

tests.name: an untouched register reads null
a set answers with the value it now holds
the larger timestamp wins whichever order the merges arrive in
equal timestamps break by replica name, so two replicas agree
every delivery order of register writes converges
elements come back sorted and without duplicates
an add concurrent with a remove survives
re-adding after a remove works, and a stale state cannot undo it
every delivery order of a mixed add and remove exchange converges

examples.title: A tie broken by the writer's name
examples.request:
an untouched register, then two writes carrying the same timestamp

./your_program.sh lww-register
value r1
set r1 red 7
set r2 blue 7
value r1
examples.note: Wall clocks tie more often than anyone expects, and two replicas that resolve a tie differently have diverged permanently. The rule has to be a total order on data both sides already hold, so the name rides along with the value.

examples.title: An element removed and added again
examples.request:
one element added, removed, then added a second time

./your_program.sh or-set
add r1 x
remove r1 x
elements r1
add r1 x
elements r1
examples.note: The second add has to mint a tag the remove never saw. A set that remembers removed *elements* rather than removed *tags* answers the empty set here and can never be talked out of it.

stages.name: RGA: a replicated sequence
hints: Topic `rga`: every element has an id and points at the element it was inserted after
Concurrent inserts at the same position are ordered by id, consistently on every replica
A delete leaves a tombstone: later inserts may still point at it
Every delivery order of the same operations must read back the same sequence

tests.name: a sequence builds up as it is typed
inserting after root prepends
a delete takes the character out of the text
an insert after a deleted element still lands in its place
two replicas inserting at the same position converge
both replicas read back the same sequence after a longer exchange
a tombstone survives a state that predates the delete
every delivery order of inserts and deletes converges

examples.title: Typing, and then typing at the front
examples.request:
two characters typed in order, then a third inserted after `root`

./your_program.sh rga
insert r1 root a1 h
insert r1 a1 a2 i
text r1
insert r1 root a3 o
text r1
examples.note: `a3` and `a1` were both inserted after `root`, so they are siblings, and the larger id goes first. That single rule is what makes two replicas that never spoke agree on the order of characters they typed at the same spot.

examples.title: A delete leaves something behind
examples.request:
the second character is deleted, then something is inserted after it

./your_program.sh rga
insert r1 root a1 h
insert r1 a1 a2 i
delete r1 a2
text r1
insert r1 a2 a3 o
text r1
examples.note: The deleted element has to stay in the structure with a flag on it. A replica that erases it cannot place `a3` at all when this arrives from elsewhere, and the two replicas have diverged over a character nobody can see.

stages.name: Chandy-Lamport snapshots
hints: Topic `snapshot`: a process records its own state when it first sees a marker
After that it records every message arriving on a channel until that channel's marker
The snapshot's total must equal the system's total, whatever the interleaving
A process sends a marker on every outgoing channel immediately after recording

tests.name: a snapshot of a quiet system is the state the system is in
a snapshot taken while money is in flight still totals correctly
a process records its own state the first time it sees a marker and not again
a message arriving after its channel's marker is not recorded
a snapshot is complete only once every process and channel has reported
a seeded interleaving snapshots the same total every time
two snapshots in a row both total correctly
a marker started anywhere goes round a one-way ring
the reported total is the recorded balances plus the recorded channels

examples.title: A snapshot with money in the channel
examples.request:
`p1` sends 30, then `p2` starts the snapshot while that 30 is still in the channel

./your_program.sh snapshot
init p1 100
init p2 50
channel p1 p2
channel p2 p1
send p1 p2 30
snapshot p2
deliver p2 p1
deliver p1 p2
deliver p1 p2
result
examples.note: The 30 is in neither balance at the instant of the snapshot: it has left `p1` and not reached `p2`. A snapshot that records only balances loses it, which is exactly why the algorithm records channels as well.

examples.title: What the marker separates
examples.request:
a marker delivered to `p2`, and only then a payment down the same channel

./your_program.sh snapshot
init p1 100
init p2 50
channel p1 p2
channel p2 p1
snapshot p1
deliver p1 p2
send p1 p2 25
deliver p1 p2
deliver p2 p1
